title: Voices of the Early Americas, Now on Exhibit
content:
The early Americas: jade pendants, the infant Jaguar god of the Underworld, empires, gold, silver, gods, art, books, temples, pyramids, Incas, Aztecs, Olmecs, Mayas, Taínos, Nahuas, maps, pictograms, Spanish, Portuguese, French, British, Dutch, Africans and vast new nations.

This is but a smattering of “Voices of the Early Americas,” the Library’s new permanent gallery in the Jefferson Building that draws heavily on the Jay I. Kislak Collection of the Archaeology and History of the Early Americas and is complemented by other rare books, maps, photographs and modern poetry from across the Library.

The new gallery, primarily funded by the Kislak Family Foundation, is divided into four periods and in roughly chronological order. It expands and deepens an earlier Kislak exhibit and tells a more far-ranging narrative from roughly 3,000 years ago into the 21st century. Display screens stretch high overhead; an artifact wall shows many objects for the first time; and high-tech displays turn a sweeping history into an immersive experience.

title: “I Love Lucy” … in the Kitchen
content:
—This is a guest post by Ellie Hart, an archives processing technician in the Music Division. It also appears in the November/December issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Many fans know the “Pioneer Women” episode of “I Love Lucy” where Lucy and Ethel overzealously knead a ball of dough and accidentally bake a loaf of bread the size of a sofa. The real-life Lucille Ball and husband Desi Arnaz — a quintessential 1950s showbiz couple — were far more capable in the kitchen than that comic disaster suggests.

The Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz Papers, part of the collections of the Library’s Music Division, contain two cookbooks plus a cheerful jumble of loose recipes and notes — handwritten, typed or torn from magazines and newspapers — that demonstrate their skill with a skillet.

Their copy of “The Settlement” cookbook is peppered with handwritten notes by Lucille and Desi in the margins. Their own homemade, unpublished cookbook — in a volume emblazoned “Cash” — is filled with page after page of handwritten recipes for favorite dishes: stuffed bell peppers, light tea cake, persimmon cake, cheese blintzes.
